Each of my package posts has a short video near the top. A pointer drags
a slider, a menu opens, a caption explains the step. It looks like a
screen recording.

It is not one. Nothing in the video was filmed. A script asks a web page
for its state at 0 ms, then at 33 ms, then at 67 ms, and takes a picture
each time. ffmpeg joins the pictures into a video.

::: {.demo-video}
:::

This post is about how that works, and why I did it this way.

## Why not a screen recording

A screen recording records what happened. I wanted to describe what should
happen, and then draw it.

A recording has three problems for a demo that I want to keep:

- **It is never the same twice.** The pointer moves at a slightly
  different speed. A plot takes a little longer to draw. If I record again
  next month, the video changes in ways I did not ask for.
- **It needs the real app running.** The apps are R. To record them, I
  need R, the packages, the data, and a window of the right size, all at
  once.
- **A small change means a new take.** If I change the blog's font, every
  video still shows the old one. With a recording, the only fix is to
  record again by hand.

The app in the video above is a few lines of R:

```r
library(shiny)
library(rewind)

ui <- fluidPage(
  rewind_buttons(),
  selectInput("region", "Region", c("North", "South", "East", "West")),
  sliderInput("year", "Year", 2018, 2026, 2024),
  plotOutput("plot")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  rewind_enable()

  output$plot <- renderPlot(plot_for(input$region, input$year))
}
```

The video does not run this app. It shows a page that looks like it, and
that page is a function of time.

## A scene is a function of time

Each video has one HTML page, which I call a scene. The scene defines one
function, `window.renderAt(ms)`. It puts the page in the state that it has
at that moment, and it does nothing else. It does not start a timer, and
it does not wait for anything.

This is the key rule. If the page depends only on `ms`, then frame 120 is
the same picture on every run. The recorder can ask for the frames in any
order, as fast or as slow as it likes.

A scene describes its story as a timeline. Here is part of the rewind
scene, a little simplified:

```js
window.renderAt = function (ms) {
  // The drag runs from 1200 to 2200 ms. The region changes at 3650 ms.
  // Ctrl+Z at 4750 ms puts it back.
  const dragX = track(ms, [[1200, xOf(2024)], [2200, xOf(2020)]]);
  let year = ms < 1200 ? 2024 : yearAt(dragX);
  let region = ms >= 3650 ? "East" : "North";
  if (ms >= 4750) region = "North";

  // The position in the history, as a list of steps.
  const index = stepAt(ms, [[0, 0], [2600, 1], [4100, 2], [4750, 1]]);
  document.querySelector(".rewind-undo").disabled = index === 0;

  setCaption(ms, [
    [900, 2900, "One drag is one step"],
    [2950, 4350, "Changing Region is another step"],
    [4450, 5700, "Ctrl+Z steps back: Region is North again"],
  ]);
  setVeil(ms, DURATION);
};
```

Every value on the page is computed from `ms`. Nothing remembers the last
frame.

## Small helpers for time

A few small functions do most of the work. They all take the time first.

```js
// A value that goes from a to b between t0 and t1, with easing.
const tween = (ms, t0, t1, a, b) =>
  lerp(a, b, ease(clamp((ms - t0) / (t1 - t0))));

// The value of a list of [time, value] keys at a time: eased between keys.
function track(ms, keys) {
  if (ms <= keys[0][0]) return keys[0][1];
  for (let i = 1; i < keys.length; i++) {
    if (ms <= keys[i][0]) {
      return tween(ms, keys[i - 1][0], keys[i][0], keys[i - 1][1], keys[i][1]);
    }
  }
  return keys[keys.length - 1][1];
}

// The state of a list of steps, [time, value], at a time:
// the last step that has started.
function stepAt(ms, steps) {
  let value = steps[0][1];
  for (const [t, v] of steps) if (ms >= t) value = v;
  return value;
}
```

`track()` is for things that glide: the pointer, a slider handle. `stepAt()`
is for things that jump: a menu that is open or closed, the position in the
undo history. With these two, a scene reads like a script for a film: at
this time, this happens.

The parts that are not the app are drawn the same way. The pointer follows
a list of `[time, x, y]` keys and makes a ripple at each click time. The
caption is a pill that fades in and out between two times. The keys of a
shortcut, such as `Ctrl` and `Z`, appear in the corner and press down at
their time.

One more piece makes the video loop well. A white sheet covers the scene
in the first 350 ms and fades in again in the last 450 ms. The last frame
and the first frame are then both white, so the loop has no jump.

## Things that move on their own

The rule "the page depends only on `ms`" is easy to break by accident.
Three things can break it.

**CSS transitions.** A transition runs in real time, between two frames
that the recorder takes. The shared stylesheet turns them all off:

```css
*, *::before, *::after {
  transition: none !important;
}
```

**CSS animations.** The bones skeleton has a wave that moves across the
grey bars. It is a CSS animation, and it belongs in the video. So the
scene does not turn it off. It sets its time instead:

```js
// Set the time of every running animation, and hold it there.
function freezeAnimations(ms) {
  for (const a of document.getAnimations()) {
    a.pause();
    a.currentTime = ms;
  }
}
```

`document.getAnimations()` returns every animation on the page. Each one
is paused and moved to the time of the frame. The wave is then exactly
where it should be at that moment.

This matters for the bones scene in another way. Its markup and its CSS
classes are the ones that `withBones()` writes, and its stylesheet is the
real `bones.css` from the package:

```r
ui <- fluidPage(
  withBones(plotOutput("chart")),
  withBones(tableOutput("results"), rows = 8)
)
```

So the skeleton in the video is drawn by the package, not copied by hand.
Only the clock is new: `renderAt(ms)` sets the classes that the package's
JavaScript would set at that time.

**Fonts.** If the first frames are taken before the web font has loaded,
they show a fallback font, and the text jumps a few frames in. The
recorder waits for every weight of the font before it takes the first
picture.

## The recorder

The recorder is a Node script of about 100 lines. It uses Playwright to
open the scene in Chromium, and ffmpeg to make the video.

The page is 640 by 360 pixels, at a device scale of 2. The pictures are
then 1280 by 720, and the text is sharp. The script steps the clock 30
times a second and pipes each picture straight into ffmpeg:

```js
const frames = Math.round((duration / 1000) * FPS);
for (let i = 0; i < frames; i++) {
  await page.evaluate((ms) => window.renderAt(ms), (i * 1000) / FPS);
  const png = await page.screenshot({ type: "png" });
  if (!encoder.stdin.write(png)) {
    await new Promise((r) => encoder.stdin.once("drain", r));
  }
}
```

ffmpeg reads the PNGs from its input and writes an H.264 file:

```bash
ffmpeg -f image2pipe -framerate 30 -i - \
  -c:v libx264 -preset slow -crf 21 -tune animation \
  -pix_fmt yuv420p -movflags +faststart -an preview.mp4
```

`-tune animation` suits pictures with large flat areas, which is what a
user interface is. `-movflags +faststart` puts the index at the front of
the file, so the browser can start to play it before the whole file has
arrived. `-an` means no sound.

Last, the script calls `renderAt()` once more, at a time that the scene
chooses, and saves that picture as a JPEG. That is the poster: the image
that shows before the video plays. Each scene picks a moment that explains
itself. For rewind, it is the moment of `Ctrl+Z`, with both buttons in use.

## What it gives me

A video of 9 seconds is 270 frames. Each of my three videos is between
140 KB and 210 KB, smaller than most photos on a phone.

The best part came a few days ago. I changed the colours and the font of
this blog. The videos had the old caption colour and the old font. I changed
two stylesheets and ran one command. All three videos and their posters
were recorded again in under a minute, and nothing else in them changed.

On the page, the video is muted and loops, and it plays by itself where
the browser allows it. A reader who asks for less motion gets the poster
and the play button instead. In the RSS feed, which other sites such as
R-bloggers copy, there is no video at all: the feed shows the poster, with
a link to the post.

## The limits

This is not the right tool for every demo.

- **It is a recreation.** The video shows how the package behaves, not
  the R code running. If the package changes, the scene does not change
  with it. I have to keep them in step by hand.
- **A scene takes time to write.** The rewind scene is a few hundred lines
  of HTML and JavaScript. A screen recording takes a minute.
- **It cannot show real speed.** A demo of how fast something is needs the
  real thing. Here, the scene decides how long everything takes.

If you want the real app on screen, `shinytest2` can drive it and take
screenshots of it. Then the timing belongs to the app, not to a clock.
For a demo that I want to keep, change and record again, the clock wins.

## Try it

The scenes and the recorder are in the repository of this blog, in the
[`_previews` folder](https://github.com/tenmeh/tenmeh.github.io/tree/main/_previews).
You need Node, Playwright with Chromium, and ffmpeg. Then:

```bash
node _previews/record.mjs          # all scenes
node _previews/record.mjs bones    # one scene
```

If you make a demo this way, I would like to see it.
